claim: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) occurs in approximately 2–5% of children in the USA.
source: OSA occurs in approximately 2–5% of children (Marcus et al., 2012) and 33% of adults 30–69 years of age (Benjafield et al., 2019) in the USA.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marcus et al., 2012.

claim: OSA occurs in 33% of adults 30–69 years of age in the USA.
source: OSA occurs in approximately 2–5% of children (Marcus et al., 2012) and 33% of adults 30–69 years of age (Benjafield et al., 2019) in the USA.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Benjafield et al., 2019.

claim: Young children with moderate to severe OSA can develop blood pressure dysregulation.
source: Even young children with moderate to severe OSA can develop blood pressure dysregulation (Amin et al., 2004), systemic hypertension (Enright et al., 2003; Kohyama et al., 2003), and left ventricular hypertrophy (Amin et al., 2002; Amin et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Amin et al., 2004.

claim: Young children with moderate to severe OSA can develop systemic hypertension.
source: Even young children with moderate to severe OSA can develop blood pressure dysregulation (Amin et al., 2004), systemic hypertension (Enright et al., 2003; Kohyama et al., 2003), and left ventricular hypertrophy (Amin et al., 2002; Amin et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Enright et al., 2003 and Kohyama et al., 2003.

claim: Young children with moderate to severe OSA can develop left ventricular hypertrophy.
source: Even young children with moderate to severe OSA can develop blood pressure dysregulation (Amin et al., 2004), systemic hypertension (Enright et al., 2003; Kohyama et al., 2003), and left ventricular hypertrophy (Amin et al., 2002; Amin et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 2002 and Amin et al., 2005.

claim: OSA is associated with a significant socioeconomic burden in the USA.
source: OSA is associated with a significant socioeconomic burden in the USA (Sullivan, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sullivan, 2016.

claim: Cellular responses to changes in oxygen levels are primarily mediated by the hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs).
source: Cellular responses to changes in oxygen levels are primarily mediated by the hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cellular oxygen sensing mechanisms.

claim: The lung is the first organ to sense large changes in inspired oxygen levels.
source: Although the lung is the first organ to sense large changes in inspired oxygen levels, little is known about the consequences of IH to the lung HIF-responsive pathways.
evidence: This is based on the logical inference that the lung is the first organ exposed to inhaled air.

claim: Efforts to understand the effects of OSA have primarily focused on systemic inflammation.
source: Efforts to understand the effects of OSA have primarily focused on systemic inflammation (Gozal et al., 2008), oxidative stress (Tauman et al., 2014), and endothelial dysfunction (Kheirandish-Gozal et al., 2013; Bhattacharjee et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gozal et al., 2008.

claim: Efforts to understand the effects of OSA have primarily focused on oxidative stress.
source: Efforts to understand the effects of OSA have primarily focused on systemic inflammation (Gozal et al., 2008), oxidative stress (Tauman et al., 2014), and endothelial dysfunction (Kheirandish-Gozal et al., 2013; Bhattacharjee et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tauman et al., 2014.

claim: Efforts to understand the effects of OSA have primarily focused on endothelial dysfunction.
source: Efforts to understand the effects of OSA have primarily focused on systemic inflammation (Gozal et al., 2008), oxidative stress (Tauman et al., 2014), and endothelial dysfunction (Kheirandish-Gozal et al., 2013; Bhattacharjee et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kheirandish-Gozal et al., 2013 and Bhattacharjee et al., 2012.

claim: HIFs stabilized under low-oxygen conditions can affect the circadian transcriptional–translational feedback loop at the cellular level.
source: For example, HIFs stabilized under low-oxygen conditions can affect the circadian transcriptional–translational feedback loop at the cellular level (Adamovich et al., 2017; Kobayashi et al., 2017; Peek et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2017; Hogenesch et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Adamovich et al., 2017; Kobayashi et al., 2017; Peek et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2017; Hogenesch et al., 1998.

claim: Acute exposure to IH results in dysregulation of the circadian clock that is time-of-day dependent and tissue specific.
source: Even acute exposure to IH results in dysregulation of the circadian clock that is time-of-day dependent and tissue specific, and these effects persist in some tissue for up to 24 hr after exposure (Manella et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Manella et al., 2020.

claim: The effects of acute IH exposure on the circadian clock persist in some tissue for up to 24 hr after exposure.
source: Even acute exposure to IH results in dysregulation of the circadian clock that is time-of-day dependent and tissue specific, and these effects persist in some tissue for up to 24 hr after exposure (Manella et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Manella et al., 2020.

claim: Pathways involved in immune responses and regulation can be activated or suppressed in the presence of IH.
source: Pathways involved in immune responses and regulation can also be activated or suppressed in the presence of IH (Cubillos-Zapata et al., 2017; Lam and Ip, 2019), contributing to comorbid disease initiation and progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cubillos-Zapata et al., 2017 and Lam and Ip, 2019.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has emerged as a method for evaluating transcriptional states from thousands of individual cells.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has emerged as a method for evaluating transcriptional states from thousands of individual cells (Zhang et al., 2018), advancing our understanding of how specific cell types contribute to physiology and disease (Zhang et al., 2018; Plasschaert et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: scRNA-seq has advanced our understanding of how specific cell types contribute to physiology and disease.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has emerged as a method for evaluating transcriptional states from thousands of individual cells (Zhang et al., 2018), advancing our understanding of how specific cell types contribute to physiology and disease (Zhang et al., 2018; Plasschaert et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2018 and Plasschaert et al., 2018.

claim: Moderate to severe OSA is associated with interstitial lung disease with remodeling of the extracellular matrix in humans.
source: In humans, moderate to severe OSA is associated with interstitial lung disease with remodeling of the extracellular matrix (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2017.

claim: Mice were exposed to IH or room air (normoxia) for the entire 12 hr inactive phase for 9 days.
source: After 14 days of entrainment in the 12 hr:12 hr light:dark cycle, mice were exposed to IH or room air (normoxia) for the entire 12 hr inactive phase for 9 days (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol performed in this study, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining of whole lungs did not show comprehensive changes in architecture or inflammatory remodeling after exposure to IH.
source: Hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining of whole lungs did not show comprehensive changes in architecture or inflammatory remodeling after exposure to IH (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were 374 genes upregulated and 149 downregulated in mouse lung after exposure to IH (BHQ < 0.05 and fold change > 1.5).
source: There were 374 genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) upregulated and 149 downregulated in mouse lung after exposure to IH (Benjamini-Hochberg q value (BHQ) < 0.05 and fold change > 1.5).
evidence: This is a result from bulk RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The top upregulated genes in mouse lung after IH exposure included well-known HIF-1 target genes (e.g. Edn1, Bnip3, and Ankrd37).
source: Not surprisingly, the top upregulated genes included well-known HIF-1 target genes (e.g. Edn1, Bnip3, and Ankrd37; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from bulk RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, with reference to established knowledge about HIF-1 target genes.

claim: Pathways induced in response to hypoxia included circadian rhythm, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix organization.
source: Pathways induced in response to hypoxia included circadian rhythm, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix organization (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is a result from DAVID enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Several circadian clock repressors (e.g. Nr1d1, Nr1d2, Bhlhe40, and Per3) were significantly upregulated in the IH group.
source: Several circadian clock repressors (e.g. Nr1d1, Nr1d2, Bhlhe40, and Per3) were significantly upregulated in the IH group (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is a tight interaction between clock genes and HIFs.
source: As previously reported, there is a tight interaction between clock genes and HIFs (Edgar et al., 2012; Gu et al., 2000; Hogenesch et al., 1998; McIntosh et al., 2010; Taylor and Zhulin, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Edgar et al., 2012; Gu et al., 2000; Hogenesch et al., 1998; McIntosh et al., 2010; Taylor and Zhulin, 1999.

claim: Increased expression of RNAs associated with angiogenesis, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), was observed after IH.
source: Increased expression of RNAs associated with angiogenesis, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), was observed after IH, consistent with findings in a mouse model of prolonged exposure to IH (Reinke et al., 2011a) and after 72 hr of IH exposure to endothelial cells in vitro (Wohlrab et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by citations to Reinke et al., 2011a and Wohlrab et al., 2018.

claim: There is a tight relationship between angiogenesis and pulmonary hypertension.
source: There is a tight relationship between angiogenesis and pulmonary hypertension (Tuder and Voelkel, 2002), a clinical consequence associated with OSA.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tuder and Voelkel, 2002.

claim: RNAs associated with immune responses and cell cycle were significantly downregulated after 9 days of IH.
source: Unexpectedly, RNAs associated with immune responses and cell cycle were significantly downregulated after 9 days of IH (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: HIFs are important regulators of inflammation and immune responses.
source: Present findings contrast with the general concept that HIFs are important regulators of inflammation and immune responses (Eltzschig and Carmeliet, 2011; Scholz and Taylor, 2013; Taylor et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eltzschig and Carmeliet, 2011; Scholz and Taylor, 2013; Taylor et al., 2016.

claim: Activation of neutrophils by HIFs is largely considered proinflammatory.
source: For example, activation of neutrophils by HIFs is largely considered proinflammatory (Walmsley et al., 2005; Peyssonnaux et al., 2005; Taylor et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Walmsley et al., 2005; Peyssonnaux et al., 2005; Taylor et al., 2016.

claim: The cell cycle and cell division downregulation may be associated with HIFs induced in cell cycle arrest in response to IH.
source: The cell cycle and cell division downregulation may be associated with HIFs induced in cell cycle arrest in response to IH (Koshiji et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to Koshiji et al., 2004.

claim: In total, 12,324 and 16,125 pulmonary cells were sequenced from IH and control mice, respectively.
source: In total, we sequenced 12,324 and 16,125 pulmonary cells from IH and control mice, with 3542–5641 cells per biological replicate.
evidence: This is a description of the scRNA-seq data generated in this study.

claim: Unsupervised analysis identified 25 transcriptionally distinct cell clusters, corresponding to 19 distinct cell types.
source: Unsupervised analysis identified 25 transcriptionally distinct cell clusters, corresponding to 19 distinct cell types (Figure 2A,B) based on the expression of established marker genes (see Materials and methods), including stromal, epithelial, endothelial, immune, and small numbers of other cell types.
evidence: This is a result from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The proportion of endothelial, alveolar epithelial type II (AT2), and fibroblast/myofibroblast cells were modestly increased in the IH-exposed mice.
source: The proportion of endothelial, alveolar epithelial type II (AT2), and fibroblast/myofibroblast cells were modestly increased, but the proportion of immune cells (e.g. B and T cells) was decreased in the IH-exposed mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of immune cells (e.g. B and T cells) was decreased in the IH-exposed mice.
source: The proportion of endothelial, alveolar epithelial type II (AT2), and fibroblast/myofibroblast cells were modestly increased, but the proportion of immune cells (e.g. B and T cells) was decreased in the IH-exposed mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportional variation of lung cell types was small (BHQ > 0.05).
source: Overall, the proportional variation of lung cell types was small (BHQ > 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the cell type composition analysis.

claim: Confocal immunofluorescence microscopy did not demonstrate comprehensive inflammatory remodeling.
source: Similar to H and E histology, confocal immunofluorescence microscopy did not demonstrate comprehensive inflammatory remodeling.
evidence: This is a finding from the immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: Immunostaining for endothelial markers FOXF1 and LYVE1 showed modest increases in the number of endothelial cells in mice exposed to IH compared to control mice.
source: Immunostaining for endothelial markers FOXF1 and LYVE1 showed modest increases in the number of endothelial cells in mice exposed to IH (Figure 3C,D) compared to control mice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Staining for MKI67 did not show statistically significant changes in cell proliferation.
source: Also important, staining for MKI67 did not show statistically significant changes in cell proliferation (Figure 3E–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3E-H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression levels of HOPX and SFTPC in alveolar type I and II cells, respectively, were not different for IH versus control mice.
source: Expression levels of HOPX and SFTPC in alveolar type I and II cells, respectively, were not different for IH (Figure 3K,L) versus control (Figure 3I,J) mice.
evidence: This is a finding from the immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3I-L.

claim: Immunostaining for the progenitor marker SOX9 did not demonstrate any significant changes after IH exposure.
source: Immunostaining for the progenitor marker SOX9 (Figure 3I–L) or the extracellular matrix marker POSTN (Figure 3M–P) did not demonstrate any significant changes after IH exposure.
evidence: This is a finding from the immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3I-L.

claim: Immunostaining for the extracellular matrix marker POSTN did not demonstrate any significant changes after IH exposure.
source: Immunostaining for the progenitor marker SOX9 (Figure 3I–L) or the extracellular matrix marker POSTN (Figure 3M–P) did not demonstrate any significant changes after IH exposure.
evidence: This is a finding from the immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3M-P.

claim: There was a modest increase (11.5%; BHQ < 0.05) of endothelial cells in mice exposed to IH compared to controls.
source: Overall, there was a modest increase (11.5%; BHQ < 0.05) of endothelial cells in mice exposed to IH compared to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1); however, this does not necessarily reflect a biologic difference.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no comprehensive changes in alveolar area and alveolar wall thickness based on morphometric quantification for mice exposed to IH compared to controls.
source: We did not see comprehensive changes in alveolar area and alveolar wall thickness based on morphometric quantification for mice exposed to IH compared to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the morphometric analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: The average MaxFeret90 measurements and alveolar areas were 21.0 µM and 419 µM2 in mice exposed to IH.
source: The average MaxFeret90 measurements and alveolar areas were 21.0 µM and 419 µM2 in mice exposed to IH, while the average MaxFeret90 measurements and alveolar areas were 23.5 µM and 564 µM2 in control mice.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the morphometric analysis.

claim: The average MaxFeret90 measurements and alveolar areas were 23.5 µM and 564 µM2 in control mice.
source: The average MaxFeret90 measurements and alveolar areas were 21.0 µM and 419 µM2 in mice exposed to IH, while the average MaxFeret90 measurements and alveolar areas were 23.5 µM and 564 µM2 in control mice.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the morphometric analysis.

claim: The mean alveolar wall thickness was 4.81 µM for mice exposed to IH and controls.
source: The mean alveolar wall thickness was 4.81 µM for mice exposed to IH and controls.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the morphometric analysis.

claim: Diverse biological processes were up- and downregulated in different cell types in response to IH.
source: From the DAVID enrichment analysis, diverse biological processes were up- and downregulated in different cell types in response to IH (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a result from the DAVID enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Hypoxia-responsive and circadian pathways were enriched in those upregulated genes in response to IH in endothelial cells, myofibroblasts, and AT2 cells.
source: For example, hypoxia-responsive and circadian pathways were enriched in those upregulated genes in response to IH in endothelial cells, myofibroblasts, and AT2 cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: Circadian pathways were highly enriched in multiple cell populations, not just epithelial cells.
source: Surprisingly, circadian pathways were highly enriched in multiple cell populations, not just epithelial cells, a population that is important for circadian rhythmicity in the lung (Gibbs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis, with a citation to Gibbs et al., 2009 for the role of epithelial cells in lung circadian rhythmicity.

claim: Cell adhesion genes are upregulated in endothelial cells, myofibroblasts, fibroblasts, and pericytes after exposure to IH.
source: Our data demonstrate that cell adhesion genes are upregulated in endothelial cells, myofibroblasts, fibroblasts, and pericytes after exposure to IH.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression and pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: Lung endothelial and stromal cells may contribute to the increased circulating cell adhesion molecules in OSA patients.
source: These results suggest that lung endothelial and stromal cells may contribute to the increased circulating cell adhesion molecules in OSA patients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that cell adhesion genes are upregulated in these cell types.

claim: Cell adhesion molecules that control leukocyte trafficking are increased in OSA patients.
source: Interestingly, cell adhesion molecules that control leukocyte trafficking are increased in OSA patients (Ohga et al., 1999) and reduced after continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) treatment (Chin et al., 2000; Pak et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ohga et al., 1999.

claim: Cell adhesion molecules that control leukocyte trafficking are reduced after continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) treatment in OSA patients.
source: Interestingly, cell adhesion molecules that control leukocyte trafficking are increased in OSA patients (Ohga et al., 1999) and reduced after continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) treatment (Chin et al., 2000; Pak et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chin et al., 2000 and Pak et al., 2015.

claim: Immune response-related and antigen processing and presentation were enriched among those downregulated genes in monocytes, macrophages-dendritic cells, NK cells, and erythroblasts.
source: Immune response-related and antigen processing and presentation were enriched among those downregulated genes in monocytes, macrophages-dendritic cells, NK cells, and erythroblasts.
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: A hypoxic tumor microenvironment will induce immunosuppression.
source: It is known that a hypoxic tumor microenvironment will induce immunosuppression (Sitkovsky et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sitkovsky et al., 2008.

claim: Hypoxia may cause immunosuppression in patients with OSA and contribute to the increased incidence of lung cancer in this population.
source: Hypoxia may also cause immunosuppression in patients with OSA and contribute to the increased incidence of lung cancer in this population (Campos-Rodriguez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to Campos-Rodriguez et al., 2013.

claim: The response level of the same genes were different in multiple cell types.
source: As expected from specific genes in each biological process, the response level of the same genes were different in multiple cell types (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The circadian repressor gene, Nr1d1, was more responsive to IH in endothelial and AT2 cells than lymphatic endothelial cells and AT1 cells.
source: For example, the circadian repressor gene, Nr1d1, was more responsive to IH in endothelial and AT2 cells than lymphatic endothelial cells and AT1 cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Immune response genes (e.g. Iglc3, S100a8, and Oas3) decreased more in monocytes than macrophages in response to IH.
source: For example, immune response genes (e.g. Iglc3, S100a8, and Oas3) decreased more in monocytes than macrophages in response to IH.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Bleomycin-induced fibrosis is induced in mice by an Nr1d1 mutation in specific lung cells.
source: For example, bleomycin-induced fibrosis is induced in mice by an Nr1d1 mutation in specific lung cells (Cunningham et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cunningham et al., 2020.

claim: Distinct vascular endothelial cell subpopulations exist in mouse and human lung.
source: Recent studies show distinct vascular endothelial cell subpopulations in mouse and human lung (Gillich et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gillich et al., 2020.

claim: Vascular endothelial populations were annotated to endothelial artery, vein, capillary aerocytes (Cap-a), and general capillary (Cap-g) cells.
source: Our vascular endothelial populations were annotated to endothelial artery, vein, capillary aerocytes (Cap-a), and general capillary (Cap-g) cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the endothelial subpopulation analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endothelial cells demonstrated profound changes in gene expression profiles in response to IH.
source: Interestingly, we found that endothelial cells demonstrated profound changes in gene expression profiles in response to IH.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Endothelial capillary cells were more responsive to IH compared to endothelial artery and vein cells.
source: The endothelial capillary cells were more responsive to IH compared to endothelial artery and vein cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At BHQ < 0.2, more than 100 genes were significantly upregulated in aerocytes and general capillary cells.
source: For example, at BHQ < 0.2, more than 100 genes were significantly upregulated in aerocytes and general capillary cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Only one gene in the arterial endothelial cells and 57 genes in the venular endothelial cells were significantly upregulated at BHQ < 0.2.
source: However, only one gene in the arterial endothelial cells and 57 genes in the venular endothelial cells were significantly upregulated at the same cutoff.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: General capillary cells are more responsive to hypoxia than aerocytes.
source: Among the capillary cells, general capillary cells are more responsive to hypoxia than aerocytes.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Hypoxia-responsive genes (e.g. Pdk1, Vegfc, Slc2a1, Pkm, and Flt1) showed higher levels of expression variation (fold change and significance) in general capillary cells than aerocytes.
source: Hypoxia-responsive genes (e.g. Pdk1, Vegfc, Slc2a1, Pkm, and Flt1) showed higher levels of expression variation (fold change and significance) in general capillary cells than aerocytes (Figure 5C), demonstrating variation at the subpopulation level.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Aerocytes are specialized for gas exchange.
source: Aerocytes are specialized for gas exchange, and general capillary cells function in capillary homeostasis and aerocyte production during repair (Gillich et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gillich et al., 2020.

claim: General capillary cells function in capillary homeostasis and aerocyte production during repair.
source: Aerocytes are specialized for gas exchange, and general capillary cells function in capillary homeostasis and aerocyte production during repair (Gillich et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gillich et al., 2020.

claim: General capillary cells contact stromal cells while aerocytes lie in close proximity to AT1 cells.
source: For example, general capillary cells contact stromal cells while aerocytes lie in close proximity to AT1 cells (Gillich et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gillich et al., 2020.

claim: Glycolytic process was upregulated in both aerocytes and general capillary cells in response to IH.
source: Glycolytic process was upregulated and cell migration was downregulated in both aerocytes and general capillary cells in response to IH (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Cell migration was downregulated in both aerocytes and general capillary cells in response to IH.
source: Glycolytic process was upregulated and cell migration was downregulated in both aerocytes and general capillary cells in response to IH (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Changes in the glycolytic process were specific to endothelial cell types.
source: Interestingly, changes in the glycolytic process were specific to endothelial cell types (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Regulation of cell proliferation and regulation of angiogenesis were only enriched for those up- and downregulated genes in general capillary cells in response to IH.
source: For example, regulation of cell proliferation and regulation of angiogenesis were only enriched for those up- and downregulated genes in general capillary cells in response to IH.
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: Phagocytosis, immune response, and regulation of cell shape were only enriched for those downregulated genes in aerocytes.
source: While phagocytosis, immune response, and regulation of cell shape were only enriched for those downregulated genes in aerocytes (Figure 5D,E), this may reflect aerocyte's specific role in leukocyte trafficking and gas exchange, both highly influenced by exposure to IH.
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Hypoxia-associated TFs (e.g. Epas1, Jun, and Ahr), Foxf1 (canonical endothelial cell marker), and Ybx1 (glycolysis related) were among the top-ranked TFs in both aerocytes and general capillary cells.
source: Hypoxia-associated TFs (e.g. Epas1, Jun, and Ahr), Foxf1 (canonical endothelial cell marker), and Ybx1 (glycolysis related) were among the top-ranked TFs in both aerocytes and general capillary cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the SINCERA transcription factor analysis.

claim: Tbx2, Tbx3, and Meox1 were among the top-ranked TFs only in aerocytes, which are considered aerocyte-specific TFs.
source: Tbx2, Tbx3, and Meox1 were among the top-ranked TFs only in aerocytes, which are considered aerocyte-specific TFs (Gillich et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the SINCERA transcription factor analysis, with a citation to Gillich et al., 2020 for the aerocyte-specific nature of these TFs.

claim: Three immune response-related TFs (Hlx, Rarg, and Smarca2) were only top-ranked in aerocytes.
source: Interestingly, three immune response-related TFs (Hlx, Rarg, and Smarca2) were only top-ranked in aerocytes.
evidence: This is a finding from the SINCERA transcription factor analysis.

claim: Tcf4 and Sox17 were among the top-ranked TFs only in general capillary cells, which are associated with endothelial cell regeneration or stem cell self-renewal.
source: Additionally,Tcf4 and Sox17 were among the top-ranked TFs only in general capillary cells, which are associated with endothelial cell regeneration or stem cell self-renewal (van Es et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the SINCERA transcription factor analysis, with citations to van Es et al., 2012 and Liu et al., 2019 for the functional associations.

claim: Elk3 and Casz1 were among the top-ranked TFs in general capillary cells and are related to angiogenesis.
source: Elk3 and Casz1 were among the top-ranked TFs in general capillary cells and are related to angiogenesis (Heo and Cho, 2014; Charpentier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the SINCERA transcription factor analysis, with citations to Heo and Cho, 2014 and Charpentier et al., 2013 for the functional associations.

claim: OSA is associated with an array of pulmonary diseases, such as interstitial lung disease (ILD), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), and pulmonary hypertension (PH).
source: OSA is associated with an array of pulmonary diseases, such as interstitial lung disease (ILD) (Kim et al., 2017), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) (Lancaster et al., 2009), and pulmonary hypertension (PH) (Sajkov and McEvoy, 2009; Chaouat et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2017; Lancaster et al., 2009; Sajkov and McEvoy, 2009; Chaouat et al., 1996.

claim: IH led to significantly more upregulated than downregulated pulmonary disease-associated genes.
source: IH led to significantly more upregulated than downregulated pulmonary disease-associated genes (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the disease gene enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: IH-induced expression in myofibroblasts and fibroblasts demonstrated enrichment of genes associated with pulmonary fibrosis (PF).
source: IH-induced expression in myofibroblasts and fibroblasts demonstrated enrichment of genes associated with pulmonary fibrosis (PF).
evidence: This is a finding from the disease gene enrichment analysis.

claim: Ptgis is a PH-associated gene highly expressed in myofibroblasts and fibroblasts compared to other cell types.
source: For example, Ptgis is a PH-associated gene highly expressed in myofibroblasts and fibroblasts compared to other cell types (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ptgis is a target gene for epoprostenol – a drug used for treating PH.
source: Ptgis is also a target gene for epoprostenol – a drug used for treating PH (Sitbon and Vonk Noordegraaf, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sitbon and Vonk Noordegraaf, 2017.

claim: The IPF-associated gene, Thbs1, was highly expressed and more responsive to IH in myofibroblasts compared to other cell types.
source: The IPF-associated gene, Thbs1 (Idell et al., 1989; Kuhn and Mason, 1995; Yehualaeshet et al., 2000), was highly expressed and more responsive to IH in myofibroblasts compared to other cell types.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis, with citations to Idell et al., 1989; Kuhn and Mason, 1995; Yehualaeshet et al., 2000 for the IPF association.

claim: THBS1 is upregulated in lung stromal cells of patients with chronic interstitial lung diseases (e.g. IPF) compared to healthy controls.
source: THBS1 is upregulated in lung stromal cells of patients with chronic interstitial lung diseases (e.g. IPF) compared to healthy controls (Gene Explorer under Banovich/Kropski in http://www.ipfcellatlas.com/; Habermann et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Habermann et al., 2020 and reference to the IPF cell atlas database.

claim: Msr1 is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)-associated gene.
source: Msr1 (Silverman et al., 2002; Hersh et al., 2006) is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)-associated gene, which was highly expressed in macrophage-DCs, basophils, and monocytes, consistent with scRNA-seq data from patients with IPF (Gene Explorer under Banovich/Kropski in http://www.ipfcellatlas.com/; Habermann et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Silverman et al., 2002 and Hersh et al., 2006.

claim: Msr1 was highly expressed in macrophage-DCs, basophils, and monocytes.
source: Msr1 (Silverman et al., 2002; Hersh et al., 2006) is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)-associated gene, which was highly expressed in macrophage-DCs, basophils, and monocytes, consistent with scRNA-seq data from patients with IPF (Gene Explorer under Banovich/Kropski in http://www.ipfcellatlas.com/; Habermann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis, consistent with data from Habermann et al., 2020.

claim: 42 drugs used as activators or inhibitors of 23 target genes to treat pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary fibrosis, COPD, and asthma were identified.
source: We obtained 42 drugs used as activators or inhibitors of 23 target genes to treat pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary fibrosis, COPD, and asthma (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from the drug target analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Nearly one third of these drug target genes were more responsive to IH in endothelial cells compared to other cell types.
source: Interestingly, nearly one third of these drug target genes were more responsive to IH in endothelial cells compared to other cell types (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the drug target analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myofibroblasts were involved in 98 of 176 gains of interaction (BHQ = 4.28e-50).
source: Overall, myofibroblasts were involved in 98 of 176 gains of interaction (BHQ = 4.28e-50), demonstrating the significance of this cell type in early IH-associated responses (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The GSEA showed upregulation of multiple extracellular matrices (ECM)-associated pathways (e.g. ECM proteoglycans, non-integrin membrane ECM interactions, and collagen chain trimerization) in myofibroblasts after exposure to IH.
source: The GSEA showed upregulation of multiple extracellular matrices (ECM)-associated pathways (e.g. ECM proteoglycans, non-integrin membrane ECM interactions, and collagen chain trimerization) in myofibroblasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) after exposure to IH.
evidence: This is a finding from the GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: FGF signaling pathway has a tight interaction with ECM.
source: FGF signaling pathway has a tight interaction with ECM (Taipale and Keski-Oja, 1997; Ornitz and Itoh, 2015), which may be associated with activation of the FGF signaling pathway in myofibroblasts in response to IH.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Taipale and Keski-Oja, 1997 and Ornitz and Itoh, 2015.

claim: Only Dbp and Hlf were top-ranked TFs in myofibroblasts from mice exposed to IH.
source: Interestingly, only Dbp and Hlf were top-ranked TFs in mice exposed to IH (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the SINCERA transcription factor analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: IH-induced circadian dysregulation may drive the transcriptional changes in myofibroblasts.
source: These results suggest that IH-induced circadian dysregulation may drive the transcriptional changes in myofibroblasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that circadian TFs Dbp and Hlf are top-ranked in myofibroblasts from IH-exposed mice.

claim: OSA is associated with dementia.
source: OSA results from intermittent episodes of airway collapse and hypoxemia and is associated with dementia (Osorio et al., 2015), diabetes (Punjabi and Beamer, 2009), hypertension (Marin et al., 2012), heart failure (Gottlieb et al., 2010), and stroke (Valham et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Osorio et al., 2015.

claim: OSA is associated with diabetes.
source: OSA results from intermittent episodes of airway collapse and hypoxemia and is associated with dementia (Osorio et al., 2015), diabetes (Punjabi and Beamer, 2009), hypertension (Marin et al., 2012), heart failure (Gottlieb et al., 2010), and stroke (Valham et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Punjabi and Beamer, 2009.

claim: OSA is associated with hypertension.
source: OSA results from intermittent episodes of airway collapse and hypoxemia and is associated with dementia (Osorio et al., 2015), diabetes (Punjabi and Beamer, 2009), hypertension (Marin et al., 2012), heart failure (Gottlieb et al., 2010), and stroke (Valham et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marin et al., 2012.

claim: OSA is associated with heart failure.
source: OSA results from intermittent episodes of airway collapse and hypoxemia and is associated with dementia (Osorio et al., 2015), diabetes (Punjabi and Beamer, 2009), hypertension (Marin et al., 2012), heart failure (Gottlieb et al., 2010), and stroke (Valham et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gottlieb et al., 2010.

claim: OSA is associated with stroke.
source: OSA results from intermittent episodes of airway collapse and hypoxemia and is associated with dementia (Osorio et al., 2015), diabetes (Punjabi and Beamer, 2009), hypertension (Marin et al., 2012), heart failure (Gottlieb et al., 2010), and stroke (Valham et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Valham et al., 2008.

claim: RNA profiles from lungs of mice exposed to IH shared similarity with gene expression changes in human lung from patients with pulmonary disease, including PH, COPD, and asthma.
source: RNA profiles from lungs of mice exposed to IH shared similarity with gene expression changes in human lung from patients with pulmonary disease, including PH, COPD, and asthma.
evidence: This is a finding from the disease gene enrichment analysis.

claim: OSA is associated with injury to alveolar epithelial cells and extracellular matrix remodeling, key features of ILD.
source: OSA is associated with injury to alveolar epithelial cells and extracellular matrix remodeling, key features of ILD (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2017.

claim: Macrophages, dendritic cells, and NK cells were the only populations to demonstrate altered oxidation–reduction in the early stages of IH exposure.
source: In the present study, macrophages, dendritic cells, and NK cells were the only populations to demonstrate altered oxidation–reduction in the early stages of IH exposure.
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: Chronic IH in mice caused the release of free oxygen radicals in the lung.
source: It was previously demonstrated that chronic IH in mice caused the release of free oxygen radicals in the lung (Tuleta et al., 2016), effects that could be blunted with antioxidative agents (Tuleta et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tuleta et al., 2016.

claim: The effects of chronic IH on free oxygen radicals could be blunted with antioxidative agents.
source: It was previously demonstrated that chronic IH in mice caused the release of free oxygen radicals in the lung (Tuleta et al., 2016), effects that could be blunted with antioxidative agents (Tuleta et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tuleta et al., 2016.

claim: PH from chronic IH was associated with enhanced NADPH oxidase expression.
source: PH from chronic IH was associated with enhanced NADPH oxidase expression, and knockout mice lacking one of these subunits demonstrated attenuated effects of chronic IH (Nisbet et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nisbet et al., 2009.

claim: Knockout mice lacking one NADPH oxidase subunit demonstrated attenuated effects of chronic IH.
source: PH from chronic IH was associated with enhanced NADPH oxidase expression, and knockout mice lacking one of these subunits demonstrated attenuated effects of chronic IH (Nisbet et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nisbet et al., 2009.

claim: Xu et al., 2016 identified a loss of normal epithelial cells in the development of IPF.
source: For example, Xu et al., 2016 identified a loss of normal epithelial cells in the development of IPF.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2016.

claim: Single-cell profiling of bronchial epithelial cells revealed the pulmonary ionocyte as the major source of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) activity.
source: In another study using single-cell profiling of bronchial epithelial cells, the major source of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) activity, the pulmonary ionocyte, was revealed (Plasschaert et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Plasschaert et al., 2018.

claim: CFTR is the gene mutated in cystic fibrosis.
source: As CFTR is the gene mutated in cystic fibrosis, cell-specific therapies for this disease can now be evaluated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cystic fibrosis.

claim: Prostacyclin synthase (Ptgis) expression was dramatically upregulated in myofibroblasts and fibroblasts in mice exposed to IH.
source: In our mice exposed to IH, prostacyclin synthase (Ptgis) expression was dramatically upregulated in myofibroblasts and fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Therapies targeting the prostacyclin pathway are already used for patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension.
source: As a potent vasodilator and inhibitor of platelet aggregation, therapies targeting this pathway are already used for patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (Farber and Gin-Sing, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Farber and Gin-Sing, 2016.

claim: Fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) is highly expressed in AT2 cells.
source: As another example, fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) is highly expressed in AT2 cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: FGFR2 promotes alveolar regeneration in response to lung injury.
source: FGFR2 promotes alveolar regeneration in response to lung injury (Perl and Gale, 2009) and is upregulated in patients with IPF (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Perl and Gale, 2009.

claim: FGFR2 is upregulated in patients with IPF.
source: FGFR2 promotes alveolar regeneration in response to lung injury (Perl and Gale, 2009) and is upregulated in patients with IPF (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: OSA can induce injury to the lung.
source: Previous studies suggest that OSA can induce injury to the lung (Aihara et al., 2011; Lederer et al., 2009), and OSA is prevalent in patients with IPF (Lancaster et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aihara et al., 2011 and Lederer et al., 2009.

claim: OSA is prevalent in patients with IPF.
source: Previous studies suggest that OSA can induce injury to the lung (Aihara et al., 2011; Lederer et al., 2009), and OSA is prevalent in patients with IPF (Lancaster et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lancaster et al., 2009.

claim: Dysregulation of circadian gene expression was found in multiple cell types after IH exposure.
source: Although there is limited data on the role of the circadian clock in OSA (von Allmen et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019; Gabryelska et al., 2020), it may play a significant role in this disease (Entzian et al., 1996; Smith et al., 2017; Butler et al., 2015). We found dysregulation of circadian gene expression in multiple cell types.
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway enrichment analysis, with citations to prior work on circadian rhythms in OSA.

claim: BMAL1 is the key clock TF.
source: BMAL1, the key clock TF (Hogenesch et al., 1998), interacts with CLOCK (King et al., 1997) and its partner NPAS2 (Zhou et al., 1997) to activate hundreds of target genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hogenesch et al., 1998.

claim: BMAL1 interacts with CLOCK to activate hundreds of target genes.
source: BMAL1, the key clock TF (Hogenesch et al., 1998), interacts with CLOCK (King et al., 1997) and its partner NPAS2 (Zhou et al., 1997) to activate hundreds of target genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to King et al., 1997.

claim: BMAL1 interacts with NPAS2 to activate hundreds of target genes.
source: BMAL1, the key clock TF (Hogenesch et al., 1998), interacts with CLOCK (King et al., 1997) and its partner NPAS2 (Zhou et al., 1997) to activate hundreds of target genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 1997.

claim: BMAL1, CLOCK, and NPAS2 are members of the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH)-PER-ARNT-SIM (PAS) TF family.
source: All three are members of the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH)-PER-ARNT-SIM (PAS) TF family.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the classification of these transcription factors.

claim: The HIFs (1–3) are members of the bHLH-PAS TF family.
source: The HIFs (1–3) are members of the same TF family and are stabilized under low-oxygen conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the classification of HIFs.

claim: Alterations in expression of clock genes are reported in peripheral blood cells from patients with OSA.
source: Alterations in expression of clock genes are reported in peripheral blood cells from patients with OSA (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2019.

claim: Changes in expression of clock genes in blood cells from OSA patients are not affected by CPAP treatment.
source: These changes in expression in blood cells are not affected by CPAP treatment (Moreira et al., 2017), suggesting that they persist despite treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moreira et al., 2017.

claim: The circadian clock in alveolar epithelial cells impacts pulmonary physiology.
source: It is known that the circadian clock in alveolar epithelial cells impacts pulmonary physiology, and its disruption can contribute to disease in animal models (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Disruption of the circadian clock in alveolar epithelial cells can contribute to disease in animal models.
source: It is known that the circadian clock in alveolar epithelial cells impacts pulmonary physiology, and its disruption can contribute to disease in animal models (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: IH leads to intertissue circadian misalignment (including in the lung) in mice.
source: More importantly, IH leads to intertissue circadian misalignment (including in the lung) in mice (Manella et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Manella et al., 2020.

claim: Circadian clock dysfunction may be an important early-stage consequence of hypoxia-driven disease.
source: Our findings suggest that circadian clock dysfunction may be an important early-stage consequence of hypoxia-driven disease and may contribute to downstream processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of circadian pathway dysregulation in the study.

claim: IH induced epithelial cell proliferation in lungs in some prior murine models.
source: For example, IH induced epithelial cell proliferation in lungs (Reinke et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reinke et al., 2011a.

claim: Some IH models produced increased lung volumes.
source: These models also produced other phenotypic changes, such as increased lung volumes (Reinke et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reinke et al., 2011b.

claim: In a bleomycin-induced lung injury model, fibrosis in mouse lung is worsened by IH.
source: In a bleomycin-induced lung injury model, fibrosis in mouse lung is worsened by IH (Gille et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gille et al., 2018.

claim: Short-term exposure to IH did not result in changes to the parenchyma or vessels.
source: In our model, short-term exposure to IH did not result in changes to the parenchyma or vessels.
evidence: This is a finding from the histological analysis.

claim: Models of IH can produce vascular and metabolic disturbances associated with OSA, such as sympathetic dysregulation.
source: Both models can produce vascular and metabolic disturbances associated with OSA, such as sympathetic dysregulation (Chalacheva et al., 2013; Ferreira et al., 2020), changes in blood pressure (Crossland et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2014), and metabolic dysregulation (Li et al., 2005; Jun et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chalacheva et al., 2013 and Ferreira et al., 2020.

claim: Models of IH can produce changes in blood pressure.
source: Both models can produce vascular and metabolic disturbances associated with OSA, such as sympathetic dysregulation (Chalacheva et al., 2013; Ferreira et al., 2020), changes in blood pressure (Crossland et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2014), and metabolic dysregulation (Li et al., 2005; Jun et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Crossland et al., 2013 and Schulz et al., 2014.

claim: Models of IH can produce metabolic dysregulation.
source: Both models can produce vascular and metabolic disturbances associated with OSA, such as sympathetic dysregulation (Chalacheva et al., 2013; Ferreira et al., 2020), changes in blood pressure (Crossland et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2014), and metabolic dysregulation (Li et al., 2005; Jun et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2005 and Jun et al., 2014.

claim: Chronic exposure to IH has been shown to induce lung growth in adult mice.
source: Chronic exposure to IH has also been shown to induce lung growth in adult mice (Reinke et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reinke et al., 2011b.

claim: Endothelial cells showed the most prominent transcriptional changes among all cell types in response to IH.
source: Among all cell types, endothelial cells showed the most prominent transcriptional changes.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Upregulated genes in myofibroblast cells were enriched for genes associated with pulmonary hypertension.
source: Upregulated genes in myofibroblast cells were enriched for genes associated with pulmonary hypertension and included targets of several drugs currently used to treat chronic pulmonary diseases.
evidence: This is a finding from the disease gene enrichment analysis.

claim: Upregulated genes in myofibroblast cells included targets of several drugs currently used to treat chronic pulmonary diseases.
source: Upregulated genes in myofibroblast cells were enriched for genes associated with pulmonary hypertension and included targets of several drugs currently used to treat chronic pulmonary diseases.
evidence: This is a finding from the drug target analysis.
